newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico military steps from shadows to fight drugs.
newsitem.headline: Mexico military steps from shadows to fight drugs.

text.p: Mexico's military, for decades an institution that has shunned the spotlight, is increasingly taking a high-profile role in the fight against a multi-billion dollar drug trade and a wave of violent crime.

President Ernesto Zedillo this week tapped Army Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo to head Mexico's main anti-narcotics agency as part of a larger cabinet reshuffle that sent opposition politician Antonio Lozano packing as attorney general.

Gutierrez's appointment was the latest in a series of unprecedented moves by Zedillo that have raised the army's profile in a nation where generals have long kept to the political sidelines, allowing for decades of uninterrupted civilian rule unknown by most other Latin American nations.

"It is the most significant of the recent changes. Everyone is focusing on the change in attorney general, but this move has many more implications," said Roderic Camp, a Tulane University professor who has long studied Mexico and its military.
Earlier this year, Zedillo picked another army general, Enrique Salgado, to head Mexico City's police force and slow rising violent crime, some by the police itself.

Although Salgado was not the first military man in Mexico to head up the capital's police, he was the first to fire dozens of top civilian police officials and replace them with military officers, analysts said.

Adding to their heightened role, Mexico's army has also been called on in the last few years to control increasing guerrilla violence throughout the country, first with Zapatista rebels in southern Chiapas state and this year with rebels of the Popular Revolutionary Army in central states.

Together with stepped-up military spending and better salaries for generals, Zedillo's moves have created some fear the army is getting too powerful. Late in 1995, unfounded rumours of a military coup briefly roiled financial markets.
This week's move signals Zedillo is relying more on the military in the drug war, as well. Zedillo has said the drug trafficking is the main threat to Mexico's stability.

Mexico has long been a main conduit for drugs funnelled to the United States from drug-growing regions in South America. U.S. officials estimate up to three-fourths of the cocaine entering the United States comes through Mexico, generating some $10 billion to $15 billion a year in profits.

"The real battle for control of Mexico is in the drug war ... and while a general in charge will not by itself resolve the problem, it does indicate an effort to do something more," Reforma newspaper columnist Sergio Sarmiento wrote this week.

Sarmiento said the president has turned to the military because civilian police forces are hopelessly corrupt. Earlier this year, ex-attorney general Lozano fired more than 700 federal police for corruption, mostly drug related.

As a former regional military commander based in Mexico's second city of Guadalajara, home to some of the country's toughest drug cartels, Gutierrez won a reputation as a successful drug-trade fighter.
But Camp added he believes Zedillo's increasing reliance on the military for security matters is mistaken. He also said many top generals feel uncomfortable with their new role.
"You basically are sending a message to your citizens that civilian leadership is incapable of resolving these problems, and needs the military," Camp said.
"It won't take long before the military is just as compromised as the police. There is too much money involved. And a compromised military is a dangerous institution."

There have already been signs in Mexico the army has been tainted by the drug war. A secretary of the navy was fired in 1990 by ex-President Carlos Salinas amid allegations of involvement in the drug trade.
And in 1992, nine federal police agents were killed -- and some executed -- by army troops who were defending a drug shipment on a remote airstrip in Veracruz state.
